# Recursion Without Reference:

# A Cross-Disciplinary Framework for Detecting Structural Embedding in

# Nonhuman Acoustic Signals

Jenny M. Michlich, AM1,2,3

1Department of Animal Behavior and Welfare, Husson University, Bangor, ME, USA

2School of Complex Adaptive Systems, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA 3Department of Biology, Community College of Allegheny County, Pittsburgh, PA, USA

Corresponding author: Jenny M. Michlich, michlichj@husson.edu

DRAFT — theoretical framing paper

## Abstract

Recursion has occupied a central and often contested place in debates over the evolutionary

origins of language, largely because comparative research has treated it as inseparable from

syntax and, in turn, from semantics. This coupling has made recursion difficult to test directly in

nonhuman acoustic signals: existing evidence comes almost entirely from operant

grammar-learning paradigms that assess whether an animal can discriminate a recursive grammar

under training, rather than from analysis of whether recursive structure is present in naturally

produced vocalizations at all. This paper proposes a structural, cross-disciplinary definition of

recursion — hierarchical embedding of self-similar units — that is deliberately decoupled from

any requirement that those units carry symbolic or referential meaning. Building on this

definition, I distinguish five acoustically testable embedding topologies — center-embedded,

tail-end embedded, left-boundary embedded, external (prefix) phrase expansion, and internal

phrase expansion — propose indexical semantics (rather than symbolic reference) as the

appropriate default explanation for any correlation between recursive structure and context, and

lay out four operational commitments — segmentation criteria, a self-similarity metric, an

embedding-topology test, and a null model — needed to make recursion a measurable property

of a naturalistic acoustic signal. I then describe how existing and in-development analytical

methods, including recursive contour analysis, wavelet decomposition, and the

MOMEL/INSTINT contour-modeling pipeline, can be triangulated to implement this framework,

and derive a set of falsifiable predictions that follow from treating recursion as a domain-general

property of hierarchically organized motor sequences rather than a language-specific syntactic

device.

## 1. Introduction

Since Hauser, Chomsky, and Fitch (2002) proposed that recursion may be the single

computational property that most cleanly distinguishes the human faculty of language in the

narrow sense from communicative capacities shared with other species, comparative research has

largely approached recursion as though it were inseparable from syntax, and by extension from

semantics. That framing produces a difficult testing situation: whenever something recursion-like

is reported in a nonhuman signal, it tends to be received either as evidence of incipient

proto-language or dismissed as an artifact of low-level statistical pattern matching, because the

analytical tools used to look for it are themselves borrowed wholesale from linguistic syntax,

leaving no other outcome available to report.

The empirical picture has moved in interesting directions since then. Fitch and Hauser (2004)

found that cotton-top tamarins could learn finite-state (regular) grammars but failed at

phrase-structure grammars requiring center-embedding, which looked at the time like a genuine

species boundary. Gentner, Fenn, Margoliash, and Nusbaum (2006) complicated the picture by

reporting that European starlings could recognize recursive AnBn patterns under training, and

Corballis (2007) used that result to mount a sustained challenge to the claim that recursion is

unique to human language rather than a more general property of hierarchical cognition. Suzuki,

Wheatcroft, and Griesser (2016) later described compositional syntax in Japanese tit alarm-call

sequences, adding further texture to the sense that structural properties once assumed exclusive

to human language may have partial analogues elsewhere in the animal kingdom.

What is largely missing from this literature is an account of recursion, at the level of the acoustic

signal itself, that does not already presuppose the analytical apparatus of syntax. The existing

evidence base comes from grammar-learning paradigms: trained discrimination tasks that assess

whether an animal can tell an AnBn sequence from an AnBm sequence under laboratory

conditions. These tasks are informative about a cognitive capacity for pattern discrimination, but

they do not tell us whether the vocal signal an organism produces on its own, outside of any

experimental grammar, contains embedded, self-similar structure in the first place. A negative

result in a grammar-learning task does not rule out recursive structure in the naturalistic signal,

and there is currently no standard method for looking for it directly.

This paper proposes a different starting point. Rather than beginning from syntax and asking

whether an animal can learn one, I propose to define recursion structurally — as the hierarchical

embedding of self-similar units — independent of whether those units carry any semantic

payload, and independent of whether the producing organism could, in principle, pass a

grammar-learning task in the laboratory. The goal is to make recursion something that can be

looked for directly in naturalistic acoustic recordings using contour- and wavelet-based analysis,

rather than something that can only be inferred indirectly from operant discrimination

performance. Sections 2 and 3 develop the conceptual case for this decoupling; Section 4

translates it into four operational commitments; Section 5 describes analytical methods,

including one already in active development, capable of meeting those commitments; Section 6

derives predictions the framework generates; and Section 7 situates the proposal relative to the

existing grammar-learning literature and addresses its principal limitations.

## 2. Recursion as a Cross-Disciplinary Construct

Before recursion can be operationalized for bioacoustic analysis, it is worth being explicit about

how differently the term is already used across fields, because each usage carries different, often

unstated assumptions about what recursion requires.

●​ Linguistics (syntax). Recursion is the embedding of a phrase within a phrase of the same

category — a relative clause nested inside a noun phrase, for instance — producing

potentially unbounded hierarchical depth. The formal machinery for this sense of

recursion traces back to Chomsky's (1955/1975) doctoral dissertation, which specified

generative grammars as systems of recursive rewrite rules capable of producing

unbounded structure from a finite rule set; Hauser, Chomsky, and Fitch (2002) later

proposed this same property as the candidate boundary between the human faculty of

language and the communicative capacities of other species.

●​ Music theory (contour). Melodic contours can nest smaller motivic units within larger,

self-similar phrase structures, a formal device studied on its own terms, independent of

any propositional content the melody might or might not carry.

●​ Mathematics (set theory, geometry). Recursion is a function defined in terms of itself,

applied to progressively smaller instances of a problem — the generative logic behind

fractal geometry, where self-similarity holds across scales.

●​ Topology and dynamical systems. Recursive, self-similar structure appears in

scale-invariant systems, and recursive relationships are discussed in some treatments of

topological structure in quantum mechanics.

●​ Computer science (automata theory). Recursion is a property of formal languages and of

the computational machinery required to parse them. The Chomsky hierarchy

distinguishes regular, context-free, and context-sensitive grammars precisely by the

computational resources — finite-state automaton, push-down automaton, or more —

needed to generate them, which is the formal backbone underlying the tamarin and

starling studies discussed above.

What is common across all five usages is a purely structural definition: self-similar or

hierarchically nested units, defined independent of what those units mean. What is not common

to all five — and enters only when recursion is discussed in a specifically linguistic register — is

any requirement that the nested units carry reference, intention, or symbolic content. Lin (2019)

describes this kind of cross-field transplantation as "tool migration": the movement of a

mathematical or computational construct into a new domain, where it often gains or loses

assumptions along the way. Recursion looks like a clear case of this. Linguistics imported a

structural, computational construct and then, over time, treated its own semantic baggage —

propositional meaning, external reference — as though that baggage were part of the construct

itself, rather than a separate property that happens to co-occur with recursive syntax in the

particular case of human language.

The framework developed in the remainder of this paper is, in effect, an attempt to un-migrate

the construct back toward its structural core: recursion as hierarchical embedding of self-similar

units, testable at the level of the acoustic signal, without a prior commitment to whether, or how,

those units mean anything at all.

## 3. Theoretical Framework: Decoupling Structural Recursion from Semantics

### 3.1 Five embedding topologies

Recursion is not a single structural pattern but a family of related ones, and distinguishing among

them is the first step toward a testable definition. Five topologies, in particular, are worth

separating out before recursion can be tested empirically on an acoustic signal.

●​ Center-embedded (A [B [C] B] A). A unit is nested within a larger unit of the same type,

with material from the outer unit surrounding it symmetrically on both sides at each level

of embedding. Acoustically, this would appear as a contour or motif nested inside a larger

contour, flanked on both sides by material drawn from the same higher-order category.

●​ Tail-end embedded (A [B C] [B C] [B C] …). An initial unit is followed by a fixed

unit-pair that is repeated and appended at the tail, extending the sequence without adding

embedding depth at each step. Acoustically, this looks like an initial element followed by

iterative, self-similar repetition or elaboration at the edge of a call bout, rather than

material surrounding a nested core.

●​ Left-boundary embedded (A [B [C [D]]]). Rather than nesting symmetrically or simply

chaining at the tail, each new unit is embedded one level deeper than the last, with depth

accumulating progressively and asymmetrically rather than being flanked by a matching

outer closure. This produces a cascading, single-sided embedding structure —

schematically a tree that grows deeper at one boundary with each additional unit —

distinct from center-embedding's symmetric bracketing and from tail-end embedding's

flat concatenation.

●​ External (prefix) phrase expansion ([X Y] [X Y] [Basic phrase]). A fixed "basic phrase"

core is left structurally unaffected, while recursive material is added externally, as

repeated prefix units front-loaded before that core. The recursion here operates entirely

outside the boundary of the phrase being expanded, rather than modifying its internal

structure.

●​ Internal phrase expansion ([P X Y X Y S]). Here the basic phrase's outer boundary (P …

S) stays fixed, and recursive material is inserted within that fixed frame rather than

prepended outside it. This is structurally the mirror image of external expansion: the

phrase's edges are stable and the recursion happens internally, between them.

These five topologies also differ in provenance. Center-embedding, tail-end embedding, and

left-boundary embedding are the topologies most directly addressed by existing recursive

contour analysis frameworks (Carter-Ényi, 2016). External and internal phrase expansion, by

contrast, are concepts originating in Rothstein's (1989) and Koch's (1793/1983) analyses of

musical phrase structure, incorporated into the phonological recursion literature by Schreuder

and Gilbers (2004; see also Schreuder, 2011). Including them here is deliberate: a topology being

imported from music theory rather than one already addressed by an existing bioacoustic method

is a reason to include it in the taxonomy this paper proposes, not a reason to leave it out.

These five types are not competing definitions of recursion but different structural signatures a

recursive process can leave in a signal, and distinguishing them converts an impressionistic

judgment ("this sounds recursive") into a structural question answerable from the signal itself: is

a candidate unit flanked symmetrically (center-embedded), does it simply extend a sequence via

a repeated tail unit (tail-end embedded), does embedding depth accumulate asymmetrically at

one boundary (left-boundary embedded), does recursive material sit outside an otherwise fixed

core (external phrase expansion), or is it inserted inside a fixed frame (internal phrase

expansion)? Section 4 returns to how these five questions are operationalized, and Section 5

describes how existing contour-analysis methods can be adapted to test for each.

### 3.2 Where semantics fits, if at all

Two possibilities are worth distinguishing for what, if anything, recursive acoustic structure

might represent. The first is that recursion in acoustics carries no semantic content whatsoever —

that it is a byproduct of motor-level pattern generation, the same neural machinery responsible

for hierarchically organized movement sequences more generally, applied here to the vocal

apparatus, with no representational function attached. The second is that recursion in acoustics

carries indexical semantics: the recursive pattern reliably indexes an internal or contextual state

— arousal, urgency, individual identity — without requiring reference to an external entity or

compositional combination of meaningful parts. The term itself has roots in Peirce's (1878)

semiotics and was formalized for phonetics by Abercrombie (1967), who used it for vocal

variation that “comes and goes according to [a speaker's] physical or mental state” rather than

forming part of the linguistic message being conveyed.

I take the position that indexical semantics is the more parsimonious default explanation for any

observed correlation between recursive acoustic structure and context, and that it should be the

null hypothesis ruled out before anything language-like is claimed. This matters analytically, not

just philosophically: a finding that recursive structure correlates with arousal state is not, on its

own, evidence for proto-syntax. It is evidence for indexical signaling, a communicative function

shared broadly across vertebrates and phylogenetically far older than anything resembling

compositional reference. Treating a correlation of this kind as evidence for symbolic or

referential semantics — rather than as ordinary indexical signaling — is one of the most

common failure modes in this literature, and making indexical semantics the required default is

intended specifically to block that inferential shortcut.

This proposal has a direct parallel elsewhere in the primate communication literature. Locke

(2021) argues that decades of comparative research prioritized calls that looked referential —

most prominently vervet monkey alarm calls, whose symbolic status did not hold up under later,

more rigorous re-analysis (Price et al., 2015) — while underweighting the vocal and other cues

that carry indexical information about a caller's identity, condition, and disposition: what

Goffman (1959) distinguished as information “given off” rather than “given,” and what Rendall

and Owren (2013) describe as a biological code conveying age, sex, body size, identity,

emotional state, and physical condition. Locke's broader claim is that this indexical channel, not

the search for referential symbolism, is where the strongest continuity between human and

nonhuman primate vocal communication is actually found. The present framework's insistence

on indexical semantics as the default explanation for recursive acoustic structure is the same

methodological correction applied to a different phenomenon: just as alarm-call research risked

overinterpreting agitated, reflexive vocalizations as proto-language, recursion research risks

overinterpreting a structural correlation with arousal as proto-syntax when a substantially older

and better-evidenced indexical explanation is available first.

## 4. Operationalizing Recursion for Acoustic Signals

Translating the structural definition above into something usable on real recordings requires four

commitments, made in advance of analysis rather than after the fact.

### 4.1 Segmentation criterion

A candidate recursive unit must first be defined as a discrete, repeatable acoustic segment — for

example, a pitch or amplitude contour bounded by silence, a formant trajectory bounded by

articulatory landmarks, or an inflection point in spectral entropy. Without a principled,

pre-specified segmentation criterion, any post hoc grouping of acoustic material into "units" risks

manufacturing the very recursive pattern the analysis sets out to test for.

### 4.2 Self-similarity metric

A quantitative similarity measure — dynamic time warping distance between contour shapes,

cross-correlation of spectral envelopes, or similarity of wavelet coefficients across scales — must

be specified in advance, together with a similarity threshold, in order to distinguish "the same

unit, repeated or nested" from "a different but acoustically adjacent unit." Leaving this judgment

to visual inspection of a spectrogram reintroduces exactly the impressionistic problem the

framework is meant to avoid.

### 4.3 Embedding topology

The five topologies defined in Section 3.1 must be distinguished operationally by structural

criteria applied to the segmented signal, rather than inferred impressionistically from the overall

shape of a spectrogram: whether a candidate unit is flanked symmetrically by higher-order

material on both sides (center-embedded), whether it simply extends the sequence via a repeated

tail unit (tail-end embedded), whether embedding depth accumulates progressively at one

boundary without a matching outer closure (left-boundary embedded), whether recursive

material sits outside an otherwise unaffected core (external phrase expansion), or whether it is

inserted within a fixed outer frame (internal phrase expansion).

### 4.4 Null model

Any claim of recursive structure requires a null distribution against which to test it: a Markov

chain, or a randomly permuted sequence built from the same inventory of acoustic units, so that

observed recursion frequency can be judged against what non-recursive concatenation of the

same building blocks would produce by chance. This guards against the more general risk of

mistaking any statistically structured, non-random sequence for evidence of hierarchical

embedding specifically — a signal can differ reliably from a random baseline without containing

recursion in the sense defined here, and the null model is what keeps those two claims separate.

Together, these four commitments only make sense if recursion is treated as a gradient,

measurable property of a signal rather than a binary property inferred impressionistically from a

spectrogram or established indirectly through a trained discrimination task. That shift is the

central methodological break this paper is proposing relative to the grammar-learning paradigms

that have dominated the literature to date.

## 5. Analytical Framework

Two existing bioacoustic analysis methods map reasonably well onto the operational

commitments above, and a third — already in active development as part of related work —

extends them further.

### 5.1 Recursive Contour Analysis (Carter-Ényi, 2016)

Originally developed for tonal and prosodic contour analysis, this method auto-segments a signal

based on a defined set of acoustic features — pitch, pitch change, ingressive/egressive

patterning, amplitude, duration, and timing — and searches for recursive patterning directly

within the resulting contour representation, with segmentation and annotation typically carried

out in ELAN. This satisfies the segmentation commitment in Section 4.1 directly, and provides a

natural basis for testing the embedding-topology commitment in Section 4.3, since individual

contour segments can be evaluated against all five topologies — checked for symmetric flanking,

tail repetition, progressive one-sided depth, external prefixing, or internal insertion relative to a

stable core.

### 5.2 Wavelet analysis with area maps

Wavelet decomposition represents a signal simultaneously across multiple time-frequency scales,

which makes it well suited to the self-similarity commitment in Section 4.2 — the defining

property of both center-embedding and fractal-style recursive structure more generally.

Area-map representations of wavelet coefficients render cross-scale self-similarity visually and

quantitatively tractable in a way that a single-scale spectrogram cannot.

### 5.3 The MOMEL/INSTINT pipeline

MOMEL (Modélisation de MELodie) stylizes an intonational contour into a small set of target

points, and INSTINT extends this into an algorithm for automatically detecting perceptually

relevant contour targets without manual annotation. This pipeline was developed for modeling

intonational contours generally, not for recursion detection specifically, but it directly satisfies

the segmentation commitment in Section 4.1 — a principled, automated reduction of a contour

into its target points — and could plausibly be extended to test which of the five topologies in

Section 3.1 a sequence of target-point-defined units exhibits across a longer vocal bout. Because

this pipeline is already in active development, it represents the most immediately available route

### 5.4 Triangulation

Combining contour-based segmentation for defining candidate units, wavelet analysis for testing

cross-scale self-similarity, and a null model built from randomized concatenations of the same

unit inventory would together constitute a reasonably rigorous test of structural recursion — one

that neither presupposes a grammar-learning paradigm nor requires any prior claim about the

semantic status of the units involved.

## 6. Predictions

If recursion is a domain-general property of hierarchically organized motor sequences, rather

than a device specific to linguistic syntax, several predictions follow directly from the framework

above, independent of any particular species or dataset.

●​ Recursive structure, where present, should correlate more strongly with indexical or

arousal-related acoustic parameters — amplitude, pitch range, timing irregularity — than

with any evidence of referential specificity, consistent with the indexical-semantics

account in Section 3.2.

●​ Center-embedded and left-boundary embedded structures, being computationally more

demanding than tail-end embedded or external/internal phrase expansion, should be rarer

across taxa than the latter, and where they do occur should be concentrated in species or

call types already independently associated with greater vocal flexibility.

●​ If recursive acoustic structure depends on hierarchically organized motor control rather

than on purely acoustic or aerodynamic constraints, its emergence over ontogeny should

track the maturation of motor cortical control of the vocal apparatus rather than somatic

growth alone — a developmental rather than a purely anatomical trajectory.

●​ Recursive structure detected by the contour- and wavelet-based methods in Section 5

should be reproducible across independent, reasonable segmentation choices. A signal

that appears recursive only under one particular, arbitrarily chosen segmentation scheme

is more likely an artifact of that scheme than a genuine structural property — which is

## 7. Discussion

### 7.1 Relation to the grammar-learning literature

This framework does not take a position on whether any given species "has" recursion in the

Hauser-Chomsky-Fitch sense — a syntax capable of unbounded, structure-dependent

embedding. That question is deliberately bracketed here, because it cannot be answered by

acoustic analysis alone: it requires demonstrating that an organism can generalize a pattern to

genuinely novel instances, which is a claim about cognitive capacity, not about the acoustic

signal. What this framework offers instead is a principled way of describing the signal itself, so

that a claim like "this call sequence shows recursive structure" becomes falsifiable against a

specified null model, rather than resting on spectrogram-reading intuition.

This also clarifies the relationship between the present proposal and results like those of Fitch

and Hauser (2004) and Gentner et al. (2006). Those studies asked whether an animal could learn

to discriminate a recursive grammar under operant training — a claim about a cognitive capacity

for grammar learning. The present framework asks a different, and in a sense prior, question:

whether recursive structure exists in the naturally produced signal at all, regardless of whether

the producing organism could pass a grammar-learning task in the laboratory. These questions

are complementary rather than competing, and conflating them is part of why the broader

recursion debate has proven difficult to resolve. A negative result in a grammar-learning

paradigm does not rule out recursive structure in the naturalistic signal, and a positive finding of

recursive acoustic structure does not, on its own, establish a grammar-learning capacity.

### 7.2 Limitations

The framework is agnostic about production mechanism. As formulated here, it cannot

distinguish recursion that arises from centrally organized motor hierarchies from recursion that

arises as an incidental byproduct of peripheral — aerodynamic or biomechanical — constraints

on the vocal apparatus. Resolving that distinction would require pairing the acoustic analysis

proposed here with independent kinematic or neurophysiological data, which falls outside the

scope of a purely acoustic, structural framework and is left for future work.

There is also a more general risk, inherent to any similarity-based method, of finding "recursion"

wherever self-similarity happens to exist for non-recursive reasons — simple repetition without

genuine embedding, or convergent acoustic constraints that produce similar-sounding units

without any hierarchical relationship between them. This is precisely why the null model

specified in Section 4.4 is treated as a required commitment rather than an optional check:

without it, the framework would be as vulnerable to overinterpretation as the

spectrogram-reading intuitions it is meant to replace.

## 8. Conclusion

Recursion has been difficult to study in nonhuman acoustic signals largely because it has been

treated as inseparable from syntax, and syntax as inseparable from semantics. This paper has

argued for pulling those three apart: defining recursion structurally, as hierarchical embedding of

self-similar units; treating indexical semantics, rather than symbolic reference, as the default

explanation for any correlation between recursive structure and context; and specifying four

operational commitments — a segmentation criterion, a self-similarity metric, an

embedding-topology test, and a null model — needed to make recursion a measurable rather than

an impressionistic property of a signal. Existing contour- and wavelet-based analysis methods,

together with the MOMEL/INSTINT pipeline already under development, provide a practical

route to implementing this framework on real recordings. The resulting predictions are falsifiable

and independent of any particular species, which is the central advantage of starting from

structure rather than from syntax: it gives recursion somewhere to be found, or not found, in the

signal itself.
